subject: Physics
title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism Lab
summary: Trace magnetic field lines through bar and horseshoe magnets, build an electromagnet, and see how currents, fields and motion push and power each other. Predict first, then watch what really happens.

scenarios.title: The Field Table
scenarios.setup: A bar magnet and a horseshoe magnet on a table, with a compass you can place anywhere. Field lines are drawn through the magnet so you can see where they go.

trials.prompt: The compass is on the line through the bar magnet, just beyond its North end. Predict which way the compass needle's North end points.

options.label: Away from the magnet, along its axis
Towards the magnet, along its axis
Parallel to the magnet, towards its South end
Parallel to the magnet, towards its North end

trials.outcome: It points straight away from the magnet.
trials.explanation: Outside a magnet the field runs from the North pole round to the South pole. Just beyond the North end it points away from the magnet, and a compass needle's North end follows the field.

variants.prompt: The compass is on the line through the bar magnet, just beyond its North end. Predict which way the compass needle's North end points.

options.label: Away from the magnet, along its axis
Towards the magnet, along its axis
Parallel to the magnet, towards its South end
Parallel to the magnet, towards its North end

variants.outcome: It points straight away from the magnet.
variants.explanation: Outside a magnet the field runs from the North pole round to the South pole. Just beyond the North end it points away from the magnet, and a compass needle's North end follows the field.

variants.prompt: The compass is beside the middle of the bar magnet. Predict which way the compass needle's North end points.

options.label: Parallel to the magnet, towards its South end
Parallel to the magnet, towards its North end
Away from the magnet, at right angles to it
Towards the magnet, at right angles to it

variants.outcome: It points along the magnet, towards the South end.
variants.explanation: Outside the magnet the field lines run from the North pole to the South pole. Beside the middle they run parallel to the magnet, pointing towards its South end, and the needle's North end follows them.

variants.prompt: The compass is on the line through the bar magnet, just beyond its South end. Predict which way the compass needle's North end points.

options.label: Towards the magnet, along its axis
Away from the magnet, along its axis
Parallel to the magnet, towards its South end
Parallel to the magnet, towards its North end

variants.outcome: It points straight towards the magnet.
variants.explanation: Field lines enter the magnet at its South pole. Just beyond the South end the field points back towards the magnet, and the needle's North end follows it.

variants.prompt: The compass is just to the side of the bar magnet's North end. Predict which way the compass needle's North end points.

options.label: Pointing away from the North pole
Parallel to the magnet, towards its South end
Parallel to the magnet, towards its North end

variants.outcome: It points away from the North pole, curving round towards the South.
variants.explanation: Field lines leave the North pole in all directions and then curve round to the South pole. Close to the North end the field points away from the pole, and the needle's North end follows it.

variants.prompt: The compass is in the gap between the two ends of a horseshoe magnet. Predict which way the compass needle's North end points.

options.label: Straight across the gap, from the North pole to the South pole
Along the gap, towards the bend
Out of the gap, away from both poles
It does not point anywhere in particular

variants.outcome: It points straight across the gap, from North to South.
variants.explanation: A horseshoe magnet brings its two poles close together, so between them the field lines run straight across the gap from the North pole to the South pole. That makes the field strong and uniform there.

trials.prompt: Can you find a point near the bar magnet where two of its field lines cross each other?

options.label: Yes: they cross near the poles, where they are closest together
Yes: they cross beside the middle of the magnet

trials.outcome: No crossing anywhere. The scene found 0 crossings.
trials.explanation: If two field lines crossed, a compass at that point would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible. The field has exactly one direction at every point, so field lines never cross.

variants.prompt: Can you find a point near the bar magnet where two of its field lines cross each other?

options.label: Yes: they cross near the poles, where they are closest together
Yes: they cross beside the middle of the magnet

variants.outcome: No crossing anywhere. The scene found 0 crossings.
variants.explanation: If two field lines crossed, a compass at that point would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible. The field has exactly one direction at every point, so field lines never cross.

variants.prompt: Can you find a point in or near the horseshoe magnet's gap where two field lines cross each other?

options.label: Yes: they cross in the middle of the gap
Yes: they cross near the bend

variants.outcome: No crossing anywhere. The scene found 0 crossings.
variants.explanation: The field has one direction at each point, so a compass in the gap points one way only. Lines in the gap run side by side across it; they never cross.

variants.prompt: Two bar magnets are pushed together with their North poles facing each other. Do any field lines cross in the space between them?

options.label: Yes: lines from the two North poles cross in the gap
No: the lines bend away from each other and never cross
The lines join up into single lines across the gap

variants.outcome: No crossing. The lines from the two North poles bend aside and run apart.
variants.explanation: Like poles repel, and their field lines push apart. Between them the field cancels at one point and the lines curve away on both sides. Because the field has one direction at each point, lines never cross.

variants.prompt: Outside a bar magnet, which way do the field lines run?

options.label: From the North pole round to the South pole
From the South pole round to the North pole
In closed circles around the middle of the magnet, never touching the poles

variants.outcome: They run from the North pole, round the outside, and into the South pole.
variants.explanation: By convention a field line shows the direction a compass needle's North end would point. Outside the magnet that is away from the North pole and towards the South pole; the lines carry on through the inside from South to North to form closed loops.

variants.prompt: Where the field lines of a bar magnet are packed most closely together, what is the field like?

options.label: The field is the same strength everywhere

variants.outcome: The lines bunch up at the poles, where the field is strongest.
variants.explanation: Field lines are drawn closer together where the field is stronger. They crowd together at the poles and spread out far away, so the field is strongest at the poles.

trials.prompt: Point A is just beyond the North end of the bar magnet. Point B is beside the middle of the bar magnet. Where is the magnetic field stronger?
trials.outcome: Stronger at A: about 5.9 times stronger there. The field lines are closer together at A.
trials.explanation: The field is strongest where the field lines are closest together, which is near the poles. It weakens quickly with distance, so the nearer point is stronger.

variants.explanation: The field is strongest where the field lines are closest together, which is near the poles. It weakens quickly with distance, so the nearer point is stronger.

variants.outcome: Stronger at A: about 17.4 times stronger there. The field lines are closer together at A.

trials.prompt: You cut a bar magnet in half. What do you get?

options.label: Two smaller magnets, each with its own North and South pole
One piece that is only North and one only South
Two pieces that are no longer magnets

trials.outcome: Two smaller magnets, each with a North and a South pole.
trials.explanation: Poles always come in pairs. Cutting a magnet gives two complete magnets, each with a North and a South pole.

options.label: Two smaller magnets, each with its own North and South pole

variants.prompt: A compass needle's North end points towards the Earth's geographic North. So what kind of magnetic pole is there?

options.label: Neither: the Earth has no magnetic poles

variants.outcome: A magnetic South pole.
variants.explanation: Opposite poles attract. The needle's North end is pulled to geographic North, so there must be a magnetic South pole there.

variants.prompt: You sprinkle iron filings around a bar magnet. Where do they bunch up most?
variants.outcome: Near the poles.
variants.explanation: The field is strongest near the poles, and each filing becomes a tiny magnet, so more of them cling there.

variants.prompt: The North pole of one magnet is brought close to the North pole of another. What happens?
variants.outcome: They repel.
variants.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

variants.prompt: Which of these is attracted to a magnet?
variants.outcome: An iron nail.
variants.explanation: Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials. Copper and wood are not attracted.

scenarios.title: The Electromagnetism Bench
scenarios.setup: A battery, a switch, a straight wire, a compass, an iron nail with copper wire to wind round it, and a box of paper clips.

trials.prompt: A straight wire runs North–South just above a compass, with the needle pointing North under it. You switch on 3 A with the current flowing towards the North. What does the needle do?

options.label: The needle's North end swings towards the West
The needle's North end swings towards the East

trials.outcome: The needle deflects: its North end swings towards the West (about 27°).
trials.explanation: A current makes a magnetic field that circles the wire. Under a wire carrying current to the North the field points West, so the needle turns towards the West. This was Oersted's discovery: electric currents make magnetic fields.

variants.prompt: A straight wire runs North–South just above a compass, with the needle pointing North under it. You switch on 3 A with the current flowing towards the North. What does the needle do?

options.label: The needle's North end swings towards the West
The needle's North end swings towards the East

variants.outcome: The needle deflects: its North end swings towards the West (about 27°).
variants.explanation: A current makes a magnetic field that circles the wire. Under a wire carrying current to the North the field points West, so the needle turns towards the West. This was Oersted's discovery: electric currents make magnetic fields.

variants.prompt: The same wire and compass. You reverse the battery so 3 A now flows towards the South. What does the needle do?

options.label: The needle's North end swings towards the West
The needle's North end swings towards the East

variants.outcome: The needle deflects the other way: its North end swings towards the East.
variants.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field circling the wire, so the needle swings the other way.

variants.prompt: Now the wire runs North–South underneath the compass instead of above it, with 3 A flowing towards the North. What does the needle do?

options.label: The needle's North end swings towards the West
The needle's North end swings towards the East

variants.outcome: The needle deflects towards the East, the opposite way to when the wire was above it.
variants.explanation: The field circles the wire. Above the wire it points the opposite way to below it, so putting the compass on the other side of the wire reverses the deflection.

variants.prompt: The wire is turned to run East–West above the compass, so it crosses the needle at right angles, and 3 A is switched on. What does the needle do?

options.label: The needle's North end swings towards the West
The needle's North end swings towards the East

variants.outcome: The needle does not move.
variants.explanation: Under an East–West wire the field runs North–South, along the needle, so it has nothing to turn it. The deflection happens when the wire runs along the needle, North–South.

variants.prompt: A 3 A current in the wire 3 cm above the compass deflects the needle by 27°. You raise the current to 6 A, keeping the wire at 3 cm. By roughly what angle does the needle now deflect?
variants.outcome: About 45°: twice the current gives twice the field.
variants.explanation: The wire's field is proportional to the current, so doubling the current doubles the sideways field. The needle turns until the wire's field and the Earth's field balance: tan θ doubles, from 0.5 to 1, so θ = 45°.

trials.prompt: You wind the copper wire 20 times round the iron nail and switch on 1.5 A. The nail picks up 9 paper clips. Now you switch the current off. How many clips stay on the nail?
trials.outcome: None: all the clips fall off at once.
trials.explanation: An electromagnet is only magnetic while a current flows. When the current stops, the field disappears and the soft iron nail loses its magnetism straight away. A permanent magnet would keep its clips.

variants.prompt: You wind the copper wire 40 times round the iron nail and switch on 1 A. (With 10 turns and 1 A the nail picks up 3 clips.) How many paper clips do you predict it picks up?
variants.outcome: About 12 clips. They drop off the moment you switch off.
variants.explanation: The strength of the electromagnet grows with both the number of turns and the current. 40 turns and 1 A is 4 times the reference, so about 4 × 3 = 12 clips. Switch the current off and the magnetism vanishes, so all the clips fall.

trials.prompt: A compass sits next to the tip of the electromagnet. You swap the battery's connections so the current flows the other way round the coil. What happens to the compass?

The needle stays as it was

trials.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the electromagnet's poles: the tip that was a North pole becomes a South pole, so the compass needle turns right round.

variants.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the electromagnet's poles: the tip that was a North pole becomes a South pole, so the compass needle turns right round.

variants.prompt: With 20 turns and 1.5 A the electromagnet picks up 9 clips. You double the number of turns to 40, keeping the same current. About how many clips does it pick up?
variants.outcome: About twice as many: 18.

variants.prompt: With 20 turns and 1.5 A the electromagnet picks up 9 clips. You double the current to 3 A, keeping 20 turns. About how many clips does it pick up?
variants.outcome: About twice as many: 18.

They are always stronger than any permanent magnet

trials.explanation: An electromagnet is only magnetic while current flows, so the crane can pick up scrap and let it go whenever it wants.

scenarios.title: Motors and Generators
scenarios.setup: A current-carrying rod between two magnet poles, and a separate coil of wire joined to a galvanometer with a bar magnet to move through it.

trials.prompt: A rod carries a current up the screen. The magnetic field between the poles points to the right. Use Fleming's left-hand rule. In which direction does the rod move?
trials.outcome: The rod moves into the screen (away from you).
trials.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule: point your first finger along the field and your second finger along the current, at right angles. Your thumb then points the way the force pushes the rod. The force is always at right angles to both the current and the field.

trials.prompt: The rod is 0.3 m long and carries 4 A at right angles to a field of 0.5 T. Predict the force on it.
trials.explanation: F = B I L = 0.5 T × 4 A × 0.3 m = 0.6 N. The force grows with the field, the current and the length of rod in the field.

trials.prompt: You push the North pole of a bar magnet quickly into a coil joined to a galvanometer. What does the needle do?

options.label: The needle deflects the other way

trials.outcome: The needle swings to the right while the magnet moves, then returns to zero.
trials.explanation: Moving the magnet changes the magnetic field through the coil, which induces a current. A current is induced only while the magnetic field through the coil is changing. When the magnet moves, the field through the coil changes, so a voltage and current are induced. When nothing moves, the field is steady and nothing is induced.

variants.outcome: It swings to the right, about twice as far.
variants.explanation: A faster motion changes the field through the coil faster, and the induced voltage is proportional to the rate of change.

variants.prompt: Pushing the North pole into the coil at a steady speed swings the needle to the right. Now you push it in at half the speed. What does the needle do?

options.label: It swings to the right, by more
It swings to the right, by less
It swings to the right, by the same amount

variants.outcome: It swings to the right, only about half as far.
variants.explanation: A slower motion changes the field more slowly, so the induced voltage is smaller.

variants.prompt: Pushing the North pole into the 40-turn coil swings the needle to the right. You swap to a coil with 80 turns and push in just as fast. What does the needle do?

options.label: It swings to the right, by more
It swings to the right, by less
It swings to the right, by the same amount

variants.outcome: It swings to the right, about twice as far.
variants.explanation: Each turn of the coil has a voltage induced in it, and they add up: twice the turns gives twice the voltage.

variants.prompt: Pushing the North pole into the coil swings the needle to the right. Now you pull the same pole out again at the same speed. What does the needle do?

options.label: It swings to the right, by more
It swings to the right, by less
It swings to the right, by the same amount

variants.outcome: It swings to the left, by the same amount.
variants.explanation: The field through the coil now decreases at the same rate, so the induced current reverses.

variants.prompt: Pushing the North pole into the coil swings the needle to the right. Now you hold the magnet motionless inside the coil. What does the needle do?

options.label: It swings to the right, by more
It swings to the right, by less
It swings to the right, by the same amount

variants.outcome: It returns to zero and stays there.
variants.explanation: There is no change in the field, so no voltage is induced, however strong the magnet is.

trials.prompt: An electric motor works because a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force. What happens if you reverse the current?

options.label: The force on the wire reverses
There is no force any more

trials.outcome: The force on the wire reverses.
trials.explanation: The force is at right angles to the current and the field. Reversing either one reverses the force; that is how a motor's commutator keeps it turning.

variants.prompt: An electric motor works because a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force. What happens if you reverse the current?

options.label: The force on the wire reverses
There is no force any more

variants.outcome: The force on the wire reverses.
variants.explanation: The force is at right angles to the current and the field. Reversing either one reverses the force; that is how a motor's commutator keeps it turning.

variants.prompt: A bicycle dynamo has a magnet that spins next to a coil. Why does it light the lamp only while the wheel is turning?

options.label: The field through the coil is only changing while the magnet moves
The magnet gets hot and powers the lamp

variants.outcome: The field through the coil is only changing while the magnet moves.
variants.explanation: Electromagnetic induction needs a changing field. Stop the wheel and the field is steady, so the lamp goes out.

variants.prompt: A power station generator turns a coil in a magnetic field. What is being converted?
variants.outcome: Movement energy into electrical energy.
variants.explanation: A generator uses induction: turning the coil changes the field through it and induces a current. A motor does the reverse.

variants.prompt: A loudspeaker has a coil in the field of a magnet. When the amplifier sends a changing current through the coil, what happens?

options.label: The coil moves back and forth, pushing the cone and making sound
Nothing, because the field is steady

variants.outcome: The coil moves back and forth, pushing the cone and making sound.
variants.explanation: A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field feels a force. A changing current gives a changing force, which moves the cone.

variants.prompt: The left-hand rule gives the force on a current in a field. If current and field point the same way, along the wire, what is the force?
variants.outcome: Zero.
variants.explanation: The force is B I L sin θ. When the current runs along the field, θ = 0 and there is no force.

laws.name: Magnetic field lines
